explanations.answer: They serve the Baals and the Asherahs
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says they "forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs." (Judges 3:7) Those are false gods. Notice the forgetting doesn't leave an empty spot, because something else steps right in.

explanations.answer: They stop worshiping anything at all
explanations.explanation: Close, but nobody in this verse goes quiet. The text says they served the Baals and the Asherahs, which are false gods. They forgot the LORD their God and picked up other things to serve instead. I think forgetting always costs something, friend.

explanations.answer: They head back down to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this verse packs a bag, friend. The text doesn't say they go anywhere. They stay right where they are and serve the Baals and the Asherahs, false gods. Their problem isn't where they live, it's who they forgot.

explanations.answer: They serve him for eight years
explanations.explanation: Yep. After the LORD sells them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, the text says "the Israelites served him eight years." (Judges 3:8) That's a long stretch under a foreign king. Eight years is a LOT of mornings, friend.

explanations.answer: They drive him out right away
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text gets driven out right away. Israel serves Cushan-rishathaim for eight years. That's the whole picture in this verse: eight years under a king who isn't theirs. Relief comes later, and it doesn't come fast.

An ally gets a handshake, friend. This king gets service. The text says the Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim eight years, so he's the one in charge. That's not a partnership, it's a long, hard stretch.

Right. The text says, "when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel…" (Judges 3:9) After eight years of serving a foreign king, they call out. And the LORD answers by raising up a deliverer. Don't ever let anyone tell you crying out is a waste of breath.

Actually, they do cry out. The text says, "when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel…" (Judges 3:9) That happens after the eight years of serving Cushan-rishathaim. Then the LORD raises up a deliverer for them.

That's the word. The LORD delivers Cushan-rishathaim into Othniel's hand, and Othniel "prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) Othniel is Caleb's nephew, by the way, the one the LORD raised up for this job. No bargaining and no begging, just a win.

Pleading is what Israel did back in verse 9, when they cried out. Othniel's part is different. The text says he went out to war and "prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) The LORD delivered the king into Othniel's hand.

No haggling at this table, friend. The text says the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim into Othniel's hand, and Othniel "prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) That's a win, not a deal. I once tried to bargain with an oven and I lost.

I see why that one tempts you, but it's the other way around. The text says, "the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died." (Judges 3:11) So the rest lasts as long as Othniel does. It's after he dies that things turn.

That's right. The text says "the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died." (Judges 3:11) The rest holds the whole time Othniel is alive. Forty years, friend, that's a long quiet.

explanations.answer: He gives a foreign king power over Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says, "He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD." (Judges 3:12) Eglon is the king of Moab, a nation east of Israel. That's the second time in this passage a foreign king gets power over them.

explanations.answer: He gives them forty more years of rest
explanations.explanation: The forty years of rest ended when Othniel died (Judges 3:11). This time the text says the LORD gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel. Rest doesn't come back until later. I wish the forty years had come with a refill, friend.

explanations.answer: He lets it pass without a word
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The text says the LORD gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD. So He doesn't let it pass without a word. Israel ends up under a foreign king again.

That's it. "The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years." (Judges 3:14) Compare that to the eight years under Cushan-rishathaim. That's more than double the time under a king who isn't theirs.

Twelve is short by six years. The text says the Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years. That's more than double the eight years they served Cushan-rishathaim. Friend, eighteen years is a long time to wait for a change.
Thirty is a long haul, but it's too long. The text says eighteen years. Still, eighteen is plenty. The eight years under Cushan-rishathaim now look short.

True. The text says, "So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab." (Judges 3:15) Tribute is the payment a conquered people brings to the king over them. So Ehud walks right up to Eglon with a reason to be there.

They do send him. The text says, "So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab." (Judges 3:15) Tribute is the payment a conquered people brings to the king over them. That's how Ehud, son of Gera, gets in front of the king.

That's the one. The text says Ehud "strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak." (Judges 3:16) For a left-handed man, I think that's a smart spot, since his left hand reaches across for it. Later the text says he pulls it from that right thigh (Judges 3:21).

I see your thinking, since he's left-handed. But the text says Ehud strapped the sword "to his right thigh under his cloak." (Judges 3:16) I think that placement lets his left hand do the work. Later, he reaches with his left hand and pulls it from the right thigh (Judges 3:21).
The text puts it lower and to the side. Ehud strapped the sword "to his right thigh under his cloak." (Judges 3:16) Nothing about his back. Hiding a sword under a cloak takes planning, friend.

explanations.answer: I have a secret message for you
explanations.explanation: Right. Ehud says, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) A secret message is a good reason to clear a room. He's turned back from the idols near Gilgal to say it. And the king takes him seriously.

explanations.answer: I have more tribute for you
explanations.explanation: The tribute is already presented, and Ehud has sent off the men who carried it (Judges 3:18). What he says instead is, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) A secret message is what gets the king to ask for quiet. More tribute wouldn't do that.

explanations.answer: I have come to make peace
explanations.explanation: Peace talks don't begin with a secret. The text says Ehud tells the king, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) That line is what makes the king say "Silence." It's a short sentence with a lot riding on it.

Not quite. After Ehud says, "I have a word from God for you," the text says, "the king rose from his seat." (Judges 3:20) So Eglon gets up. That's a heavy part of the story, friend, and it moves fast from here.

Right. Ehud says, "I have a word from God for you," and the text says "the king rose from his seat." (Judges 3:20) So Eglon stands up. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's best to take it in slowly.

That's the word. The text says Ehud went out "closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) That's why the servants run into locked doors in the next verse. It's a small detail that matters a lot.

Nobody's standing guard here. The text says Ehud went out "closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) The locked doors are what the servants find in the next verse. Guards would have asked questions, friend.

No marks on any doors, friend. The text says Ehud went out "closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) Locked doors are what the servants find. I've locked a door behind me too, usually with my keys inside.

explanations.answer: Relieving himself in the cool room
explanations.explanation: Yes. The servants say, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room." (Judges 3:24) They find locked doors and come up with the most ordinary guess they can. I think nobody wants to be the one who knocks on that door, and that's the whole story of the waiting.

explanations.answer: Resting up in the cool room
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess for a hot day, but it's not what they say. The text says they figured, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room." (Judges 3:24) Locked doors, so they go with the ordinary explanation. That guess is what buys Ehud time.

The servants don't think anyone's in there with him. The text says they said, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room." (Judges 3:24) That's the ordinary guess they land on when they find the doors locked. A meeting would've had some noise.

That's the one. The text says, "Then they took the key and opened the doors." (Judges 3:25) They wait until they're worried, and then they use the key. What they find is their lord lying dead on the floor. That's a sober moment, friend.
No axe swinging here. The text says the servants "took the key and opened the doors." (Judges 3:25) They'd waited a while by then, and they open it the proper way. What they find inside is heavy.
Nobody breaks anything down. The text says they "took the key and opened the doors." (Judges 3:25) That's how they find their lord lying dead on the floor. It's a quiet, heavy moment.
Right. The text says, "Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited." (Judges 3:26) He passes by the idols and gets away to Seirah. All that waiting outside the doors gave him a head start.

He does get away, and it happens during the waiting. The text says, "Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited." (Judges 3:26) He passes by the idols and escapes to Seirah. The servants are still standing at the locked doors.
Yes. The text says, "he blew the ram's horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim." (Judges 3:27) A ram's horn is a loud call that carries across hills. And the Israelites come down with him.
No fire in this verse. The text says Ehud blew the ram's horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim. A horn carries over the hills and the Israelites hear it. They come down with him.

explanations.answer: He sends runners to the tribes
explanations.explanation: Nobody's running errands here. The text says Ehud blew the ram's horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim. One long sound and the Israelites come down from the hills with him.

True. Ehud tells them, "Follow me, for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand." (Judges 3:28) He doesn't say he did this himself. He points to the LORD, and the people follow him down.

He does say it. The text records Ehud telling them, "Follow me, for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand." (Judges 3:28) So the call to follow comes with those words about the LORD. Then they follow him down.

That's right. The text says they seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, "and they did not allow anyone to cross over." (Judges 3:28) A ford is a shallow spot where people can cross a river. Hold the crossings and nobody gets through.

A bridge would let people cross, and they do the opposite. The text says they seized the fords "and they did not allow anyone to cross over." (Judges 3:28) This crossing is a closed door, not an open one.

The text doesn't say anything about waiting for a surrender. They seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab "and they did not allow anyone to cross over." (Judges 3:28) Then the next verse tells what happens to the Moabites. Waiting isn't it.
Yes. The text says, "the land had rest for eighty years." (Judges 3:30) Compare that to the forty years of rest after Othniel (Judges 3:11). Eighty is double, friend.

Sixty is a good stretch, but the text says eighty. "So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years." (Judges 3:30) That's double the forty years of rest after Othniel (Judges 3:11). I could use that much rest myself.
Twenty is too short. The text says the land had rest for eighty years. That's double the forty years after Othniel (Judges 3:11). Rest on this scale is a long time, friend.

That's it. The text says Shamgar "saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad." (Judges 3:31) An oxgoad is a long pointed stick for driving oxen, so it's a farm tool. I can't even win a fight with a rolling pin, friend.

You're thinking of Samson, one of Israel's judges later on, who struck down a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:15). Shamgar's tool is different. The text says he struck down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad. (Judges 3:31)

A tent peg is in another story, friend. Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, used one (Judges 4:21). Shamgar's tool is different, because the text says he struck down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad. (Judges 3:31)
